extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and critics of literature; novelists interested in realism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for judging (and understanding) realist novels—especially the balance between realism and romantic or epic form, moral intention, characterization, and artistic method as exemplified in Zola's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to life (realism as representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should be the representation, and in no measure the misrepresentation, of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work strives to represent life truthfully rather than distort it for effect. Consider whether depictions of social conditions, vice, and everyday detail aim at truthful portrayal rather than romanticizing or sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between creed and practice (embodying an ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zola's realism was his creed, which he tried to make his deed; but he was 'too much a romanticist by birth and tradition' to exemplify realism completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an author's stated aesthetic (e.g., realism) is actually realized in the work. Look for inherited habits (romanticism, sentimentality) that undermine professed aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of epical thesis-binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of Zola's books is 'bound to a thesis' and 'epical'—the imperfection of his realism began with the perfection of his form; reality is not bound to a thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a novel forces events and characters to revolve around a single central motive or thesis in a way that falsifies the complexity of life. Prefer works that allow aberration and exception rather than those that compress life to prove a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: temple (symmetry) vs tree (organic growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: We think of beauty as implicated in symmetry... two kinds of beauty: the symmetrical (temple) and the unsymmetrical (tree). Life is more like a tree; the 'temple' effect can make art false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural choices: does the novel impose rigid symmetry and engineered balance that sacrifice organic development? Favor structures that grow naturally from the material rather than contrived symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character veracity (true to human fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zola's characterizations, if not true to the 'French fact,' are true to the human fact; his people 'live in the memory as entirely as any people who have ever lived.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters feel like real human beings with internal individuality, not caricatures or mere mouthpieces for ideas. Test reader memory/impression: do characters persist after reading as believable persons?

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' autonomy (not merely serving the author)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within his epical scheme every person was so natural that his characters seemed like characters of biography rather than fiction; they were 'free agencies, bound by no allegiance to the general frame.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine if characters act from their own motivations rather than being manipulated solely to advance the plot or author's thesis. Characters should appear autonomous and not obviously instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity and point-of-view honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: A fiction must choose its point of view and include only the things that fall within a certain scope; Zola's delusion was to suppose his fictions were not selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique claims of comprehensiveness. Good novels acknowledge limits of scope and selection; evaluate whether the work responsibly frames what it includes and omits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic shaping of detail (harmony vs mere cataloguing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though Zola reported the 'rudest noises of the street,' he was, in spite of himself, producing harmony; he was shaping details into an 'orchestral accompaniment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for how the author arranges observed particulars: are details merely amassed (journalistic cataloguing) or artistically organized to produce aesthetic effect and coherence? Strong realism still needs aesthetic shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive and moral intention (high vs low motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is such a thing as high motive and such a thing as low motive... Zola's indecency was motivated by 'anxiety for sincerity and truth' springing from pity and justice, not to allure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the author's moral intent behind depicting vice or indecency: is it to expose, shame, or instruct (high motive) rather than to titillate or exploit (low motive)? Consider whether the depiction repels or corrupts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method transparency: scientific/journalistic claim vs imaginative creation
rubrics_metrics.description: He fancied himself working like a scientist collecting specimens, but he was always working like an artist, 'creating and vivifying' rather than merely recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about method. If an author presents their work as documentary or scientific, check whether they have in fact exercised selection, invention, or poetic vivification. Be wary of rhetoric that masks artistic invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and sufficiency as historical record
rubrics_metrics.description: Zola's books 'beyond any other books have the quality that alone makes novels historical'—they include everything within their scope though they are necessarily selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a novel's utility as a record of its period by whether it convincingly portrays aspects of the era within its chosen scope. Recognize limits: a novel needn't be exhaustive but should offer truthful, illuminating particulars of its time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for indecency when ethically justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Zola's books, though often indecent, are never immoral; indecency can be a condition of portraying human nature so that it may look upon its image and be ashamed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating provocative content, weigh whether the depiction serves an ethical or reforming purpose. Indecency is defensible if it aids truthful moral critique rather than gratuitous exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/verisimilitude accuracy vs universal human truth
rubrics_metrics.description: M. Brunetiere says Zola's characters are not true to the French fact; Howells counters they are true to the human fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether fidelity to a specific national or social type is necessary for success, or whether capturing universal human realities suffices. Consider reader's expectations for local accuracy versus broader humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical engagement and public consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Zola's literary heroism (e.g., the Dreyfus affair) showed 'anxiety for sincerity and truth' that translated into public moral action and 'triumph as a humanist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the social commitment of the writer: does the work and the author's conduct engage with injustice and provoke constructive public response? Consider whether moral courage and activism enhance the work's stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of artificial 'joiner-work' in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no appearance of what M. Ernest Dupuy calls the joiner-work of the French fictionalists; Zola's final effect is joiner-work: 'It is a temple he builds, and not a tree he plants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the composition shows visible seams—artificial contrivances that join pieces together—rather than a continuous organic development. Favor prose and structure that feel seamlessly grown from material.
